items.name: 1. George Washington
facts: Commanded the Continental Army in the War of Independence before becoming the first President in 1789.
Elected unanimously by the Electoral College in 1789 and again in 1792.
Led troops in person to put down the Whiskey Rebellion in Pennsylvania in 1794.
Signed the Jay Treaty with Britain in 1795, which was deeply unpopular at home.
His Farewell Address of 1796 warned against party divisions and permanent foreign alliances.
Refused a third term and retired to Mount Vernon in 1797, setting a two-term custom.
His vice president was John Adams, who succeeded him.

items.name: 2. John Adams
facts: Washington's vice president, and the first President to lose a bid for re-election.
Signed the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798, which punished criticism of the government.
Fought an undeclared naval Quasi-War with France from 1798 to 1800.
First President to live in the White House, moving in in November 1800.
Lost the bitter election of 1800 to his own vice president, Thomas Jefferson.
Died on 4 July 1826, the same day as Jefferson, 50 years after independence.

items.name: 3. Thomas Jefferson
facts: Wrote the Declaration of Independence in 1776, long before becoming President.
The election of 1800 ended in a tie with Aaron Burr, so the House of Representatives chose Jefferson.
Bought the Louisiana Territory from France in 1803, doubling the size of the country.
Sent Lewis and Clark to explore the West from 1804 to 1806.
Fought the First Barbary War against pirates in North Africa from 1801 to 1805.
The Embargo Act of 1807 banned foreign trade and badly damaged the economy.
His vice president Aaron Burr shot and killed Alexander Hamilton in a duel in 1804.

items.name: 4. James Madison
facts: Called the Father of the Constitution for his work at the convention of 1787.
Led the country into the War of 1812 against Britain.
British troops burned the White House and the Capitol in August 1814.
The Treaty of Ghent ended the war in December 1814 with no change of borders.
Signed the charter of the Second Bank of the United States in 1816.
His wife Dolley Madison is famous for saving a portrait of Washington from the burning White House.

items.name: 5. James Monroe
facts: His presidency is known as the Era of Good Feelings because party conflict had faded.
The Panic of 1819 was the first major financial crisis of the United States.
Acquired Florida from Spain under the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819.
Signed the Missouri Compromise in 1820, balancing slave states and free states.
Ran almost unopposed for re-election in 1820, winning all but one electoral vote.
The Monroe Doctrine of 1823 warned European powers not to colonise the Americas.
Died on 4 July 1831, the third President to die on Independence Day.

items.name: 6. John Quincy Adams
facts: Son of John Adams, the second President.
No candidate won a majority in 1824, so the House of Representatives chose him over Andrew Jackson.
Jackson's supporters called it a "corrupt bargain" when Henry Clay became his Secretary of State.
As Monroe's Secretary of State he had drafted the Monroe Doctrine and won Florida from Spain.
Lost heavily to Jackson in 1828.
Later served 17 years in the House of Representatives, fighting slavery, and collapsed at his desk there in 1848.

items.name: 7. Andrew Jackson
facts: A general who beat the British at the Battle of New Orleans in January 1815.
First President from the Democratic Party, which formed around him.
Signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830, leading to the Trail of Tears.
Vetoed the renewal of the Second Bank of the United States in 1832 and withdrew its funds.
Faced the Nullification Crisis of 1832 when South Carolina rejected federal tariffs.
Paid off the entire national debt in 1835, the only time this has ever happened.
Survived the first assassination attempt on a President in 1835 when both pistols misfired.

items.name: 8. Martin Van Buren
facts: Jackson's vice president and chosen successor, nicknamed the Little Magician.
First President born a United States citizen rather than a British subject.
Grew up speaking Dutch in Kinderhook, New York; English was his second language.
The Panic of 1837 struck weeks after he took office and caused a long depression.
The Cherokee were forced west on the Trail of Tears in 1838, during his term.
Set up an independent Treasury in 1840 to keep government money out of private banks.
Lost to William Henry Harrison in 1840 and later ran for the Free Soil Party in 1848.

items.name: 9. William Henry Harrison
facts: Won fame beating Tecumseh's warriors at the Battle of Tippecanoe in 1811.
Won in 1840 with the slogan "Tippecanoe and Tyler Too" and a log cabin campaign.
Gave the longest inaugural address in history, nearly two hours, in cold weather.
Died of illness on 4 April 1841, just 31 days into his term, the first President to die in office.
His grandson Benjamin Harrison became the 23rd President.

items.name: 10. John Tyler
facts: First vice president to take over after a President's death, in 1841.
Insisted he was fully President, not just acting, setting the precedent for all later successions.
Expelled from the Whig Party in 1841 after vetoing its bank bills.
Signed the annexation of Texas in the last days of his term in 1845.
Fathered 15 children, more than any other President.

items.name: 11. James K. Polk
facts: A dark horse candidate in 1844 who promised to serve only one term and kept his word.
Settled the Oregon border with Britain at the 49th parallel in 1846.
Led the Mexican-American War from 1846 to 1848.
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848 gained California and the South West from Mexico.
Gold was discovered in California in 1848, during his term.
Died of cholera in June 1849, only three months after leaving office.

items.name: 12. Zachary Taylor
facts: A career soldier nicknamed Old Rough and Ready, who won battles in the Mexican-American War.
Had never voted in a presidential election before running in 1848.
Opposed the spread of slavery to new territories, despite owning slaves himself.
Died suddenly in July 1850, probably of a stomach illness, after about 16 months in office.
Second President to die in office; his vice president Millard Fillmore took over.

items.name: 13. Millard Fillmore
facts: Became President when Zachary Taylor died in July 1850.
Signed the Compromise of 1850, including the hated Fugitive Slave Act.
Sent Commodore Perry's fleet to Japan in 1852 to open it to trade.
The last Whig President; he ran again in 1856 for the Know Nothing Party.

items.name: 14. Franklin Pierce
facts: His only surviving son was killed in a train crash weeks before his inauguration in 1853.
The Gadsden Purchase of 1853 bought land from Mexico for a southern railway route.
Signed the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, which let settlers vote on slavery and sparked "Bleeding Kansas".
His own party refused to nominate him again in 1856.

items.name: 15. James Buchanan
facts: The only President who never married.
The Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision came two days after his inauguration in 1857.
The Panic of 1857 brought a sharp economic downturn.
Seven Southern states left the Union after Lincoln's election, between December 1860 and February 1861, and he took no action.
Often ranked as the worst President for failing to prevent the Civil War.

items.name: 16. Abraham Lincoln
facts: First Republican President, elected in 1860; Southern states seceded before he took office.
The Civil War began when Confederates fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861.
Signed the Homestead Act and the Pacific Railway Act in 1862.
Issued the Emancipation Proclamation on 1 January 1863, freeing slaves in rebel states.
Gave the Gettysburg Address in November 1863: "government of the people, by the people, for the people".
Re-elected in 1864 on a National Union ticket with Andrew Johnson, a Southern Democrat.
Shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre on 14 April 1865, days after Lee surrendered, and died the next morning.

items.name: 17. Andrew Johnson
facts: A Tennessee Democrat who stayed loyal to the Union and became Lincoln's vice president in 1865.
Took office when Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865.
Clashed with Radical Republicans in Congress over Reconstruction and the rights of freed slaves.
Vetoed the Civil Rights Act of 1866, but Congress overrode him.
Alaska was bought from Russia for 7.2 million dollars in 1867, mocked as "Seward's Folly".
First President to be impeached, in 1868; the Senate acquitted him by a single vote.
Returned to the Senate in 1875, the only former President to do so.

items.name: 18. Ulysses S. Grant
facts: The Union general who accepted Lee's surrender at Appomattox in April 1865.
The first transcontinental railway was completed in May 1869.
Signed the Fifteenth Amendment, protecting Black men's right to vote, ratified in 1870.
Used the Enforcement Acts of 1870 and 1871 to crush the Ku Klux Klan.
The Panic of 1873 began a long economic depression.
His second term was marked by scandals, including the Whiskey Ring in 1875.
Wrote his famous memoirs while dying of throat cancer, finishing days before his death in 1885.

items.name: 19. Rutherford B. Hayes
facts: Won the disputed election of 1876 by one electoral vote after a special commission ruled in his favour.
The Compromise of 1877 gave him the presidency in exchange for withdrawing federal troops from the South.
That withdrawal ended Reconstruction.
Sent federal troops to break the Great Railroad Strike of 1877.
Banned alcohol from the White House; his wife was nicknamed "Lemonade Lucy".
Kept his promise to serve only one term and did not run in 1880.

items.name: 20. James A. Garfield
facts: Nominated in 1880 as a compromise candidate on the 36th ballot of a deadlocked convention.
Shot by Charles Guiteau, a disappointed office-seeker, at a Washington railway station in July 1881.
Lingered for 79 days as doctors probed the wound with unwashed hands, and died in September 1881.
Alexander Graham Bell tried and failed to find the bullet with a metal detector.
Served only 200 days, the second shortest presidency.
His murder led to the Pendleton Act of 1883, which reformed the civil service.

items.name: 21. Chester A. Arthur
facts: Became President when Garfield died in September 1881.
Had been a New York machine politician, but surprised critics by backing reform.
Signed the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the first law banning immigration by nationality.
Signed the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act in 1883, ending the spoils system for many jobs.
Kept his kidney disease secret, did not seek a full term, and died in 1886.

items.name: 22. Grover Cleveland
facts: First Democrat elected President since the Civil War, in 1884.
Won despite a scandal over fathering a child outside marriage; opponents chanted "Ma, Ma, where's my Pa?"
Married 21-year-old Frances Folsom in the White House in 1886, the only President to wed there.
Signed the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887, the first federal regulation of railways.
Vetoed more bills in his first term than all previous Presidents put together.
Won the popular vote in 1888 but lost the Electoral College to Benjamin Harrison.

items.name: 23. Benjamin Harrison
facts: Grandson of William Henry Harrison, the ninth President.
Lost the popular vote in 1888 but won in the Electoral College.
Six new states joined in 1889 and 1890: the two Dakotas, Montana, Washington, Idaho and Wyoming.
Signed the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890, the first federal law against monopolies.
Signed the McKinley Tariff of 1890, which raised import duties to record levels.
Electricity was installed in the White House in 1891; the family feared touching the switches.
Lost the 1892 rematch to Grover Cleveland.

items.name: 24. Grover Cleveland
facts: Beat Benjamin Harrison in 1892 to return to office; the Panic of 1893 struck weeks later and caused a deep depression.
Had secret surgery for mouth cancer on a yacht in 1893 to avoid alarming the public.
Sent federal troops to break the Pullman railway strike in 1894.

items.name: 25. William McKinley
facts: Won in 1896 against William Jennings Bryan, who campaigned for free silver.
Led the Spanish-American War of 1898 after the battleship Maine blew up in Havana harbour.
The USA gained Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines from Spain, and annexed Hawaii in 1898.
Signed the Gold Standard Act in 1900.
Shot by anarchist Leon Czolgosz at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo in September 1901 and died eight days later.
Third President assassinated; Theodore Roosevelt took over.

items.name: 26. Theodore Roosevelt
facts: Became President at 42 when McKinley was assassinated in 1901, the youngest ever.
A "trust buster" who broke up big monopolies such as Northern Securities in 1904.
Began building the Panama Canal after backing Panama's independence from Colombia in 1903.
Won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906 for ending the Russo-Japanese War.
Signed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act in 1906.
Created national parks, forests and monuments, protecting about 230 million acres.
Ran again in 1912 for his own Progressive "Bull Moose" Party, splitting the Republican vote.

items.name: 27. William Howard Taft
facts: Roosevelt's chosen successor and the heaviest President, weighing well over 20 stone.
Brought more antitrust cases than Roosevelt; Standard Oil was broken up in 1911.
Congress passed the Sixteenth Amendment allowing a federal income tax in 1909; it was ratified in 1913.
Came third in the 1912 election behind Wilson and Roosevelt, who had split from him.
Later became Chief Justice of the Supreme Court from 1921 to 1930, the only person to hold both offices.

items.name: 28. Woodrow Wilson
facts: Won in 1912 when Roosevelt and Taft split the Republican vote.
Created the Federal Reserve in 1913 and signed the Clayton Antitrust Act in 1914.
Kept the USA out of the First World War until April 1917, after German submarine attacks and the Zimmermann Telegram.
Set out his Fourteen Points for peace in January 1918 and championed the League of Nations.
The Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 and 1920, so the USA never joined the League.
Suffered a severe stroke in October 1919; his wife Edith hid how ill he was.
The Nineteenth Amendment gave women the vote in 1920.

items.name: 29. Warren G. Harding
facts: Won a landslide in 1920 promising a "return to normalcy" after the war.
His administration was riddled with corruption, most famously the Teapot Dome oil scandal.
Died suddenly in San Francisco in August 1923, probably of a heart attack.
His vice president Calvin Coolidge was sworn in by lamplight by his own father, a notary.

items.name: 30. Calvin Coolidge
facts: Became President when Harding died in August 1923 and won his own term in 1924.
Nicknamed "Silent Cal" for saying very little.
Signed the Immigration Act of 1924, which sharply limited immigration using national quotas.
Said in 1925 that "the chief business of the American people is business".
Cut taxes and kept government small during the boom of the Roaring Twenties.
Chose not to run in 1928 with the words "I do not choose to run".

items.name: 31. Herbert Hoover
facts: A mining engineer who had organised food relief for Europe during and after the First World War.
The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 struck eight months after he took office.
Signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff in 1930, which worsened the world depression.
Shanty towns of the homeless were nicknamed "Hoovervilles".
Sent the army to clear the Bonus Army of veterans from Washington in 1932.
Lost in a landslide to Franklin Roosevelt in 1932.

items.name: 32. Franklin D. Roosevelt
facts: Elected four times, from 1932 to 1944, more than any other President.
Paralysed by polio in 1921, he used a wheelchair for the rest of his life.
Launched the New Deal in 1933 to fight the Great Depression, declaring "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself".
Signed the Social Security Act in 1935.
Led the USA into the Second World War after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941.
Met Churchill and Stalin at Yalta in February 1945.
Died of a brain haemorrhage at Warm Springs, Georgia, in April 1945, weeks before Germany surrendered.

items.name: 33. Harry S. Truman
facts: Became President when Roosevelt died in April 1945, after only 82 days as vice president.
Ordered the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, ending the war with Japan.
The Truman Doctrine of 1947 and the Marshall Plan of 1948 aimed to contain communism.
Ordered the Berlin Airlift in 1948 and helped found NATO in 1949.
Won a surprise victory in 1948; the Chicago Tribune wrongly printed "Dewey Defeats Truman".
Sent US troops to the Korean War in 1950 and sacked General MacArthur in 1951.
Kept a sign on his desk reading "The buck stops here".

items.name: 34. Dwight D. Eisenhower
facts: Supreme Allied Commander who led the D-Day landings in June 1944.
Ended the Korean War with an armistice in July 1953.
Signed the Interstate Highway Act in 1956, creating the national motorway network.
Sent federal troops to Little Rock, Arkansas, in 1957 to enforce school desegregation.
Set up NASA in 1958 after the Soviet Union launched Sputnik.
His farewell address in 1961 warned of the "military-industrial complex".
His vice president was Richard Nixon.

items.name: 35. John F. Kennedy
facts: At 43, the youngest person elected President, and the first Roman Catholic.
Said "ask not what your country can do for you" in his inaugural address in January 1961.
The Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba failed in April 1961.
Set the goal of landing a man on the Moon by the end of the 1960s.
Faced down the Soviet Union in the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962.
Said "Ich bin ein Berliner" in West Berlin in June 1963.
Assassinated by Lee Harvey Oswald in Dallas on 22 November 1963.

items.name: 36. Lyndon B. Johnson
facts: Sworn in aboard Air Force One hours after Kennedy was shot in November 1963.
Signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Won in 1964 with 61 per cent of the vote, the largest share in history.
His Great Society programme created Medicare and Medicaid in 1965.
Sharply escalated the Vietnam War after the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in 1964.
Announced in March 1968 that he would not seek another term as the war grew unpopular.

items.name: 37. Richard Nixon
facts: Eisenhower's vice president, who lost to Kennedy in 1960 and then won in 1968.
The first Moon landing, Apollo 11, happened in July 1969.
Set up the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970.
Visited communist China in February 1972, opening relations after decades of hostility.
Signed the Paris Peace Accords in January 1973, ending US involvement in Vietnam.
The Watergate scandal began with a burglary at Democratic headquarters in June 1972.
Resigned in August 1974 to avoid impeachment, the only President to do so.

items.name: 38. Gerald Ford
facts: Appointed vice president in 1973 when Spiro Agnew resigned, so he was never elected to either office.
Became President when Nixon resigned in August 1974.
Pardoned Nixon a month later, which badly damaged his popularity.
Saigon fell to North Vietnam in April 1975, ending the Vietnam War.
Survived two assassination attempts in September 1975, both by women in California.
Lost narrowly to Jimmy Carter in 1976.

items.name: 39. Jimmy Carter
facts: A peanut farmer and former Governor of Georgia.
Signed treaties in 1977 handing the Panama Canal to Panama by the end of 1999.
Brokered the Camp David Accords between Egypt and Israel in 1978.
The Iran hostage crisis began in November 1979 and lasted 444 days.
High inflation and petrol shortages marked his term; he gave the "crisis of confidence" speech in 1979.
Lost in a landslide to Reagan in 1980 and later won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002.
Died in December 2024 aged 100, the longest-lived President.

items.name: 40. Ronald Reagan
facts: A former Hollywood actor and Governor of California, aged 69 when elected.
Shot by John Hinckley in March 1981, just 69 days into his term, and recovered.
Cut taxes sharply in 1981, a policy known as "Reaganomics".
Called the Soviet Union an "evil empire" in 1983 and launched the Star Wars missile defence plan.
The Iran-Contra scandal of 1986 revealed secret arms sales to Iran to fund Nicaraguan rebels.
Said "Mr Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" in Berlin in June 1987.
Signed the INF Treaty with Gorbachev in 1987 to scrap intermediate-range nuclear missiles.

items.name: 41. George H. W. Bush
facts: Reagan's vice president, and before that ambassador to the UN and director of the CIA.
The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989 and the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
Sent troops to Panama in December 1989 to remove Manuel Noriega.
Signed the Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990.
Led the Gulf War coalition that drove Iraq out of Kuwait in early 1991.
Broke his 1988 pledge "Read my lips: no new taxes" and lost to Bill Clinton in 1992.
His son George W. Bush became the 43rd President.

items.name: 42. Bill Clinton
facts: Former Governor of Arkansas who beat Bush in 1992, helped by Ross Perot's third-party run.
Signed the North American Free Trade Agreement, NAFTA, in 1993.
His health care reform plan, led by Hillary Clinton, failed in 1994.
Helped broker the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland in 1998.
Oversaw a long economic boom and the first budget surpluses since 1969.
Impeached by the House in December 1998 over the Monica Lewinsky affair; acquitted by the Senate in 1999.
Led NATO's bombing of Serbia over Kosovo in 1999.

items.name: 43. George W. Bush
facts: Won the 2000 election after a Supreme Court ruling ended the Florida recount, despite losing the popular vote.
The 11 September 2001 attacks killed nearly 3,000 people and defined his presidency.
Invaded Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003.
Signed the Patriot Act in 2001 and created the Department of Homeland Security in 2002.
Signed the No Child Left Behind education law in 2002.
Hurricane Katrina devastated New Orleans in 2005 and the response was widely criticised.
The financial crisis of 2008 led to a 700 billion dollar bank bailout.

items.name: 44. Barack Obama
facts: The first Black President, elected in 2008 over John McCain.
Signed a 787 billion dollar stimulus package in 2009 to fight the Great Recession.
Won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2009.
Signed the Affordable Care Act, known as Obamacare, in March 2010.
Ordered the raid that killed Osama bin Laden in Pakistan in May 2011.
Agreed the Iran nuclear deal and the Paris climate agreement in 2015.
Restored diplomatic relations with Cuba in 2015.

items.name: 45. Donald Trump
facts: A property developer and TV star, the first President with no previous political or military office.
Beat Hillary Clinton in 2016 while losing the popular vote.
Signed large tax cuts in December 2017.
Imposed tariffs on China, starting a trade war in 2018.
The Covid-19 pandemic struck in 2020; Operation Warp Speed produced vaccines by the end of the year.
Lost to Joe Biden in 2020 and refused to accept the result; supporters stormed the Capitol on 6 January 2021.
Impeached twice, in 2019 over Ukraine and in 2021 after the Capitol riot, and acquitted both times.

items.name: 46. Joe Biden
facts: Obama's vice president and, at 78, the oldest person to become President.
His vice president Kamala Harris was the first woman to hold the office.
Withdrew US troops from Afghanistan in August 2021 as the Taliban retook Kabul.
Signed a 1.2 trillion dollar infrastructure law in 2021 and the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022.
Sent large amounts of military aid to Ukraine after Russia's invasion in February 2022.
Inflation reached a 40-year high of about 9 per cent in 2022.
Dropped out of the 2024 race in July after a poor debate performance and endorsed Kamala Harris.

items.name: 47. Donald Trump
facts: Beat Kamala Harris in November 2024, this time winning the popular vote, and returned to office in January 2025.
The first President since Grover Cleveland to serve two non-consecutive terms, and the first convicted of a felony.
Imposed sweeping tariffs on most countries in 2025, including the "Liberation Day" tariffs of April 2025.
